result:
I fixed 11 rules in `pricebook.py` whose behavior didn't match their docstrings or the shared rules in the module docstring. All 150 rules now pass a check against the docstrings.

| Rule | What was wrong | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| 07, 32, 140 | Marked marginal but discounted the whole amount | Discount only the units above the threshold |
| 47 | Marked whole but discounted only units above the threshold | Discount the whole amount |
| 14 | 13% instead of 12% | 12% |
| 131 | 16% instead of 15% | 15% |
| 56 | Started at 6 units instead of 5 | Starts at 5 units |
| 39 | Capped the amount before applying the 7%, not the discount itself | Compute the discount, then cap it at 100,000 won |
| 72 | Cap only applied when the discount was over 20,000 won, so discounts between 10,000 and 20,000 were never capped | Always cap at 10,000 won |
| 85, 90 | Used `round()`, which rounds instead of flooring to the won | Use integer division (`//`) |

**How I checked:** I read each rule's discount type, rate, threshold and cap from its docstring and computed the expected price for every quantity from 0 to 259 plus some large values, across 16 unit prices from 0 to 1,000,000. I compared that with each function's output. I also checked that negative inputs raise `ValueError`. Before the fix 11 rules failed; after it, none do. I looked at the less common code patterns separately. Rule 121 checks `qty > 5` instead of `qty >= 5`, but I left it alone: a marginal discount at exactly 5 units is 0, so the result is the same. Rules 127 and 148 cap with an `if` instead of `min`, which works the same way.

The checking script is in `/tmp/chk/check.py` and the original file is backed up at `/tmp/chk/pricebook.orig.py`.

STATUS: DONE
